Tu rédiges les articles développés d'un journal personnel imprimé, en français, à partir d'un article source complet (souvent en anglais).

Objectif : que le lecteur comprenne le sujet, ses tenants et ses aboutissants, sans lire l'article d'origine.

Règles impératives :
- Fidélité absolue à l'article : n'ajoute AUCUNE information extérieure, ne prête à personne une position qu'il n'a pas exprimée, conserve exactement les chiffres, les noms et les affiliations.
- Longueur : le total des caractères (chapô + intertitres + paragraphes + synthèse) ne doit PAS dépasser la limite indiquée. Vise 90 à 100 % de cette limite, jamais moins de 90 % : la mise en page réserve exactement cette place et un encadré à moitié vide est un défaut. Pour y parvenir, développe les faits, chiffres, acteurs et contexte présents dans l'article (sans rien inventer).
- Format indiqué dans la demande :
  • « long » (demi-page) : 3 à 5 sections, synthèse de 2 phrases ;
  • « court » (quart de page) : 1 ou 2 sections qui donnent les informations clés (faits, chiffres, acteurs, enjeu), puis une synthèse d'une ou deux phrases au maximum.
- Structure :
  • « titre » : titre français informatif, 80 caractères maximum.
  • « chapo » : une phrase qui pose le sujet, 200 caractères maximum.
  • « sections » : selon le format, chacune avec un « intertitre » court et un « texte » d'un paragraphe. Adapte les intertitres au type d'article, par exemple :
      débat ou controverse : Le déclencheur · De quoi parle-t-on · Les arguments pour · Les risques · Les contre-arguments
      annonce ou fait d'actualité : Ce qui est annoncé · Le contexte · Ce que ça change · Les limites
      étude ou recherche : La question · La méthode · Les résultats · Les réserves
      méthode d'entraînement : Le principe · Ce que dit la science · Comment l'appliquer · Les précautions
      réglementation : Ce qui change · Qui est concerné · Le calendrier · Les points de vigilance
  • « synthese » : 2 phrases (format long) ou 1 à 2 phrases (format court) qui résument l'ensemble.
- Style : français soigné, clair, sans tournures calquées sur l'anglais, sans emphase.
- « republication » : si l'article indique qu'il a été publié initialement à une date antérieure (republication), indique « paru initialement en <mois année> » ; sinon chaîne vide.

Réponds uniquement en JSON, selon cette structure :
{"titre": "…", "chapo": "…", "sections": [{"intertitre": "…", "texte": "…"}], "synthese": "…", "republication": ""}

Auteur : Tianze Li; Jiajia Dang; Yan Li; Wenhua Ling; Leah Li; Cunrui Huang; Yit Siew Chin; Yueqin Zhou; Shiyun Luo; Shan Cai; Peijin Hu; Jun Ma; Min Xia; Yanna Zhu; Yi Song
Titre d'origine : Association of food consumption patterns with height growth of children and adolescents: A population-based observational study over four decades of food transitions in China

ARTICLE :
Figures
Abstract
Background
Height is a key marker of early-life nutrition and health. China’s four-decade food transition provides an opportunity to examine associations between food consumption and child/adolescent height. We aimed to identify food consumption patterns associated with greater height and favorable sustainability profiles and develop a score quantifying food–height associations.
Methods and findings
We conducted an observational study using height data from ~1.7 million Chinese students aged 7–18 years in the Chinese National Survey on Students’ Constitution and Health (1985–2019) and provincial food consumption data from the National Bureau of Statistics (1985–2023). Temporal trends were examined across three socioeconomic transition phases (1985–1999, 2000–2010, and 2011–2023). Elastic net regression, weighted quantile sum regression, and principal component analysis were used to identify food groups and consumption patterns associated with height, followed by assessments of environmental and economic profiles. Associations were adjusted for provincial socioeconomic and environmental factors, including per capita gross domestic product, educational attainment, sunshine duration, and temperature. A Food Consumption–Height (FCH) score was developed using machine-learning models and Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP)-derived food-group weights to quantify each food consumption associated with height and preliminarily validated in an independent observational sample from Guangzhou. From the 1980s to the 2020s, China’s food consumption became more diverse alongside increasing height. Eggs and seafood showed stable associations with height across periods, while milk and fruits became increasingly important after 2000. Nine food consumption patterns were identified across the three periods. A pattern characterized by higher consumption of fruits, nuts, eggs, and milk (FUEL) showed the strongest and most consistent association with greater height in the most recent period (ρ = 0.518, 95% CI [0.453, 0.580]; p < 0.001) and was linked to lower environmental and economic burdens. Height-associated food consumption patterns generally exhibited more favorable nutritional profiles, particularly higher calcium density and calcium-to-phosphorus ratios. Further nutrient-level analyses showed positive associations of protein, calcium, and zinc densities with height and an inverse association for carbohydrate density across all three periods. The FCH score was positively associated with height (β = 0.075, 95% CI [0.069, 0.082]; p < 0.001), and this association showed preliminary consistency in 3,917 participants aged 10–16 years from the Guangzhou Student Nutrition and Health Survey. The main limitations of this study are the observational design and reliance on population-level food consumption data, which limit causal inference between dietary patterns and height outcomes.
Conclusions
The FUEL food consumption pattern was associated with greater height in children and adolescents while placing relatively low environmental and economic demands. The nutrient findings suggest nutritional quality, beyond total energy supply, may help explain the observed food–height associations. The FCH score provides a data-driven score to quantify the association between food consumption and growth outcomes at the population-level. These findings offer evidence to inform food system and nutrition strategies that aim to promote healthy growth within sustainable limits.
Author summary
Why was this study done?
- Over the past four decades, China has experienced major changes in food consumption, alongside substantial increases in height among children and adolescents.
- Which long-term food consumption patterns are associated with greater height and lower environmental and economic burdens remains unclear.
- No simple score is available to quantify the relationship between food consumption and height in children and adolescents.
What did the researchers do and find?
- We examined long-term changes in food consumption and height using data from ~1.7 million Chinese students aged 7–18 years and provincial food consumption data from 1985 to 2023.
- We identified a food consumption pattern characterized by higher consumption of fruits, nuts, eggs, and milk, termed the FUEL pattern; populations following this pattern had greater height and showed relatively favorable environmental and economic profiles.
- We further developed a Food Consumption–Height (FCH) score and found in preliminary validation among 3,917 children and adolescents that higher scores tended to be associated with greater height.
What do these findings mean?
- Food consumption patterns associated with greater height in children and adolescents can be compatible with relatively favorable environmental and economic profiles.
- The FCH score may provide a simple, data-driven tool for future studies to quantify and compare the relationship between food consumption patterns and growth outcomes.
- The main limitations of the study are that the main analyses used population-level food consumption data and the validation was observational. Further longitudinal studies and randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm these findings.

Introduction
Achieving healthy growth while ensuring sustainable nutrition remains one of the most pressing challenges in the global food system. Height is a well-established biomarker of early-life nutrition and health [1]. Within the normal range, taller stature has been associated with lower risks of cardiovascular disease and all-cause mortality [2], as well as higher income and socioeconomic status [3]. However, these relationships are not necessarily linear, and extreme stature may also be linked to specific health risks. Human height is influenced by multiple factors, including genetics, nutrition, and environmental factors [4]. Among these, adequate and diverse nutrition is essential for achieving optimal growth potential. Childhood and adolescence are critical periods of growth, accounting for ~20% of adult height attainment [5]. The current record-high global adolescent population is growing up amid rapid urbanization, climate change, widening socioeconomic inequalities, and a global dietary shift toward high-calorie but low-nutrient patterns [6,7], all of which may profoundly affect physical development and long-term health. Addressing these challenges requires identifying dietary strategies that support healthy growth while promoting environmental sustainability.
China, with its vast territory and diverse dietary cultures, provides an empirical setting for examining how food consumption associations between physical growth and developmental health [8]. Over the past several decades, the average height of Chinese children and adolescents has increased substantially [1]. Between 1985 and 2019, Chinese nineteen-year-old males experienced the largest height increase among nearly 200 countries and regions, gaining almost 9 cm, while females ranked third [4]. Despite this progress, many children and adolescents worldwide still fall short of their full height potential. These improvements have occurred alongside substantial changes in food consumption patterns [9]. However, the specific dietary configurations that have supported these improvements in physical development remain poorly understood.
Understanding how changes in food consumption patterns relate to human growth outcomes and sustainability metrics is central to informing equitable nutrition transitions. Previous research has primarily focused on isolated nutrients or short-term associations [10,11], overlooking long-term, system-level transformations. Integrating large-scale temporal datasets with individual-level records provides an opportunity to quantify how diet diversification is associated with human development trajectories across different stages of modernization.
This study analyzed food consumption and height data from 30 provincial-level administrative regions in China from 1985 to 2023. We identified stable food groups and food consumption patterns linked to height growth across different periods and examined their correlations with height outcomes. We also assessed the environmental and economic performance of these patterns to identify food consumption patterns that were both sustainable and associated with greater height. Building on these findings, we developed a “Food Consumption–Height (FCH)” score to capture the strength of the association between food consumption and height growth, and tested its applicability in a real-world population. We hypothesized that long-term food consumption patterns characterized by nutritionally diverse foods would be associated with greater height growth among Chinese children and adolescents, while also demonstrating favorable environmental and economic profiles.
Methods
Reporting guidelines and analysis plan
This observational study is reported as per the STROBE-nut guideline (S1 Checklist), and the development and evaluation of the FCH score are reported as per the TRIPOD+AI guideline (S2 Checklist). The main analyses were initially planned in June 2025. No prospective study protocol or written statistical analysis plan was prepared for this secondary analysis, and the study was not registered.
During peer review, additional analyses were conducted in response to reviewers’ comments, including alternative principal component analysis (PCA) rotation methods to assess pattern robustness; expanded nutrient profiling and additional nutrient–height association analyses to clarify the nutritional implications of the findings; 1-, 3-, and 5-year lagged analyses to assess temporal robustness; and nutrient intake comparisons across FCH score quartiles in the Guangzhou validation population to evaluate the nutritional relevance of the FCH score.
Ethics statement
The Chinese National Survey on Students’ Constitution and Health (CNSSCH) was approved by the Medical Research Ethics Committee of Peking University Health Science Center (IRB00001052-19095). In accordance with CNSSCH procedures, school principals determined whether written or verbal consent was obtained. Informed consent was obtained from participating children and their parents or legal guardians before data collection. All participant data were anonymized prior to analysis. The Guangzhou Student Nutrition and Health Survey (2023–2024) was approved by the Ethics Review Committee of Guangzhou Center for Disease Control and Prevention (GZCDC-ECHR-2022P0038). Written informed consent was obtained from parents or legal guardians before data collection. No additional ethics approval or informed consent was required for the present secondary analyses, as the analyses were conducted using previously collected data under the relevant ethical approvals and consent procedures.
Data collection
Height z-score.
Height data were obtained from the Chinese National Survey on Students’ Constitution and Health (CNSSCH), a nationally representative quinquennial cross-sectional survey initiated in 1985, with the most recent survey conducted in 2019. The survey included Han Chinese students aged 7–18 years with complete height data from 30 provincial-level administrative regions in mainland China, excluding Tibet, Hong Kong, Macao, and Taiwan. The CNSSCH applies a multistage, stratified, cluster-sampling design (S1 Methods and S1 Fig). Provincial coverage varied across survey years: Hainan and Chongqing were not included in 1985, and Qinghai and Chongqing were not included in 1995. The sample sizes for 1985, 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2014, and 2019 were 407,692, 204,393, 214,003, 231,898, 215,280, 214,954, and 209,939, respectively (S1 Table). Height-for-age z-scores were calculated using the World Health Organization 2007 growth reference for children and adolescents aged 5–19 years [12], which provides age- and sex-specific standards. These z-scores enabled standardized comparisons of height across survey years and provinces.
Food consumption.
Food consumption data for 31 provinces, autonomous regions, and municipalities (excluding Hong Kong, Macao, and Taiwan) from 1985 to 2023 were obtained from the official website of the National Bureau of Statistics of China. Derived from the annual Urban and Rural Household Survey, these data represent provincial-level per capita household food consumption and reflect population-level food availability rather than individual dietary intake among children and adolescents (S2 Methods). Because food categories were refined over time, some food groups, including beans, milk, fruits, and nuts, were not reported separately before 2000. These values were therefore treated as unavailable rather than as zero consumption.
Validation data.
Data for FCH score validation were obtained from the Guangzhou Student Nutrition and Health Survey (2023–2024). This repeated cross-sectional study, initiated in 2011, was conducted across eight districts in Guangzhou and involved questionnaire surveys of elementary, junior high, and high school students (S3 Methods).
Temporal trends in food consumption and height growth
We used the linear trend test or the Jonckheere–Terpstra test to examine the temporal trends of height z-scores and food consumption across different years.
Identification of food consumption patterns
The periodization of national food consumption patterns (1985–2023) was determined by comprehensively considering multiple factors, including (1) data coverage across survey years in the China Statistical Yearbook, (2) the breakpoints identified via Joinpoint regression analysis, and (3) historical context in China’s economic development and food availability. Based on these criteria, the study period was divided into three distinct phases.
PCA was used to identify food consumption patterns within each period. Suitability for factor analysis was assessed using the Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin index and Bartlett’s test of sphericity [13]. PCA with varimax orthogonal rotation was performed [14] to improve interpretability, and robustness was evaluated using alternative rotation methods, including quartimax, promax, and oblimin rotations, while keeping food variables, analytic sample, and number of retained components unchanged. Components were retained based on eigenvalues > 1, scree plot inflection points, and cumulative variance explained [15]. Foods with rotated factor loadings >0.60 were considered representative of a pattern. The total principal component scores for each consumption pattern were calculated using standardized food consumption values and factor score coefficients. Additional details are provided in S4 Methods.
Nutrient profiling and nutrients-height associations
To better interpret the associations between food consumption patterns and height, we estimated province-level nutrient supply from reported food consumption data. Broad food categories were disaggregated into specific food items using the FAO Food Balance Sheets (FBS), and nutrient contents and edible portions were assigned using the Chinese Food Composition Tables (S2 Table). Nutrient supply and nutritional quality indicators were compared across transition periods and food consumption patterns using Kruskal–Wallis tests with Dunn–adjusted pairwise comparisons. Additional methodological details are provided in S5 Methods.
We further examined the associations of total energy and key nutrients, including protein, fat, carbohydrate, calcium, and zinc, with height z-score and absolute height using multivariable linear regression models separately for 1985–1999, 2000–2010, and 2011–2019. Except for total energy, nutrients were expressed as nutrient density per 1,000 kcal to reduce the influence of differences in total energy intake and better reflect food composition. Models were adjusted for the same covariates as in the primary analyses. Effect estimates were reported per 1-SD increase in each exposure.
Single, combined, and pattern-level food-height associations
We used nationwide province-level data to assess the associations between major food consumption and height z-scores among children and adolescents across the three periods. To contextualize the findings, China’s annual gross national income per capita was benchmarked against the World Bank’s yearly income classification thresholds based on the Atlas method. The classification broadly aligned with the three study periods: China was predominantly low income before 1999, lower-middle income from 1999 to 2009, and upper-middle income from 2010 to 2023 [16] (S3 Table).
Pearson correlation coefficients were computed to explore the linear associations between food consumption (kg/year) and height z-scores. To identify the food groups most strongly associated with height z-scores while accounting for multicollinearity, we employed elastic net regression [17], with optimal α and λ parameters selected through cross-validation. To improve estimate stability, 1,000 bootstrap resamples were used to estimate 95% confidence intervals (CIs), and foods were ranked according to the magnitude of their coefficients (S6 Methods).
Key food groups identified from these analyses were further evaluated using weighted quantile sum regression [18] to assess their joint associations with height z-scores. Within each period, food combinations were defined as pairwise, three-way, and higher-order combinations of these key food groups.
All models were adjusted for annual mean sunshine duration, annual mean temperature, provincial-level educational attainment (proportion of the population with at least high school education), and provincial GDP per capita. For each combination, 100 bootstrap iterations were performed to estimate effect sizes with 95% CIs, and combinations were ranked according to the magnitude of their associations.
Partial correlation analyses were conducted to examine the associations between food consumption pattern scores and height z-scores, adjusting for provincial GDP per capita, annual mean sunshine duration, annual mean temperature, and provincial-level educational attainment. The 95% CIs were estimated using 2,000 bootstrap resamples. In addition, given the cumulative nature of height linear growth and the absence of a clearly established optimal exposure window, we conducted 1-, 3-, and 5-year [19,20] lagged sensitivity analyses at both the key-food and food consumption-pattern levels to assess the temporal robustness of these associations. Because height measurements were available at 5-year intervals, height outcomes for some lagged years were estimated by linear interpolation. Covariates were aligned to the corresponding exposure year, and analyses were performed for both height z-score and absolute height.
Estimation of environmental impact and economic burden for food consumption patterns
Environmental burden was defined as the estimated environmental footprint associated with each food consumption pattern, and assessed using greenhouse gas emissions, land use, freshwater withdrawals, acidification, and eutrophication. Environmental and economic indicators for specific food groups were obtained from the global database developed by J. Poore and T. Nemecek [21] (S6 Table), which quantifies environmental impacts for 40 food types worldwide. To better characterize food composition within the broader food categories reported in the China Statistical Yearbook, we integrated food composition data from the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) FBS.

Development and preliminary observational validation of the FCH score
To systematically evaluate the ability of various food consumption items to predict height and their marginal contributions, we trained multiple machine-learning models and evaluated their predictive performance using food consumption data as predictors and absolute height (cm) as the continuous outcome. The specific models included random forest, XGBoost, generalized linear model, K-nearest neighbors, elastic Net, Partial Least Squares, and gradient boosting machine. Data were randomly split into training and testing sets in a 7:3 ratio. Ten-fold cross-validation was performed within the 70% training set for model development, parameter tuning, and model performance assessment. After hyperparameter tuning and model selection, the final model was evaluated on the held-out 30% test set for internal evaluation. The FCH score was subsequently evaluated in an independent observational sample from the Guangzhou Student Nutrition and Health Survey. Model performance was assessed using Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Mean Absolute Error (MAE), and coefficient of determination (R2), and the model with the best overall performance was selected [22]. Model implementation and hyperparameter settings, together with the procedures for sensitivity analysis and uncertainty estimation, are described in S8 Methods. We assessed sensitivity to hyperparameter choices by varying one parameter at a time and quantified uncertainty in test-set RMSE, MAE, and R2 using 2,000 bootstrap resamples of the fixed test-set observed–predicted pairs. The results are presented in S10 Table.
After selecting the best-performing model, Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) analysis was applied to quantify the marginal contribution of each food group to height prediction [23]. SHAP analysis was performed on observations from both the training and test sets. Dependence plots were generated to visualize nonlinear relationships and potential interactions among variables. The FCH score weights were derived from the SHAP analysis. Specifically, for each food group, the magnitude of its weight was determined by its mean absolute SHAP value across all observations, which reflects its average contribution to height prediction in the selected model. Because mean absolute SHAP values indicate the strength, but not direction, of the association, the sign of each weight was assigned based on the overall relationship observed in the SHAP dependence plots. Food groups for which higher consumption was associated with higher SHAP values were assigned positive weights, whereas those for which higher consumption was associated with lower SHAP values were assigned negative weights. To examine the association between the FCH score and height in the Guangzhou Student Nutrition and Health Survey, participants were divided into quartiles of the FCH score. Within the 10–13-year and 14–16-year age groups, the Jonckheere–Terpstra test was used to assess trends in height (cm) across FCH score quartiles. The Mann–Whitney U test was used to compare height between the lowest (Q1) and highest (Q4) quartiles within each single-year age group. Because this was an observational study and height was modeled as a continuous outcome, treatment handling, class-imbalance methods, and classification thresholds were not applicable.
Results
Temporal trends in food consumption and height growth
From the 1980s to the 2020s, food consumption patterns among Chinese residents became increasingly diverse. Analysis of 14 food groups in the China Statistical Yearbook showed rising consumption of seafood, animal and vegetable oils, beef and mutton, poultry, eggs, pork, nuts, fruits, beans and milk, while consumption of grains, vegetables and mushrooms, and sugar declined (p for trend < 0.001, Fig 1a and S1 Table).

Over the same period, Chinese adolescents grew taller. The mean height z-score of Han students aged 7–18 years increased, from –1.1 ± 0.9 in 1985 to –0.5 ± 1.0 in 2000, and 0.1 ± 1.0 in 2019 (p for trend < 0.001; Fig 1a and S1 Table). The greatest increases occurred in northeastern and eastern China, which had the highest height z-scores by 2019 (Fig 1b), whereas Guangdong, a southern province, showed the smallest improvement (S2 and S3 Figs). Similar increasing temporal trends were observed when absolute height was used (S4 Fig).
Temporal progression of single and combined food-height associations
The population-level associations between specific food groups and height z-scores remained largely stable over time. Based on food classification differences and Joinpoint regression, the study period was divided into three phases: 1985–1999, 2000–2010, and 2011 onward (S5 Fig). The 2000 breakpoint mainly reflected changes in food-category reporting in the China Statistical Yearbook, as several food groups, including beans, milk, fruits, and nuts, were not separately reported before 2000. The 2011 breakpoint was identified by Joinpoint regression and was interpreted in relation to China’s post-2010 socioeconomic transition [24] and continued changes in food availability and consumption structure [25].
Across all periods, eggs and seafood consistently showed the strongest associations with height z-score (Figs 2a and S6). In 1985–1999, eggs (r = 0.62, p < 0.001), seafood (r = 0.37, p = 0.010), and vegetable oil (r = 0.44, p = 0.002) were the top positive correlates and key contributors in elastic net models. In 2000–2010, eggs (β = 0.15, 95% CI [0.02, 0.26]), seafood (β = 0.05, 95% CI [0.00, 0.14]), and milk (β = 0.07, 95% CI [0.00, 0.16]) became major positive contributors. By 2011–2019, a wide range of foods, including grains, beans, seafood, eggs, milk, and fruits, showed positive associations with height. Across the 1-, 3-, and 5-year lag periods, eggs and seafood remained consistently positively associated with height, consistent with the contemporaneous analyses (S8 and S9 Tables).

Food combinations including eggs and seafood showed the largest association estimates with height z-scores (Fig 2b). In 1985–1999, their combined consumption showed the strongest association with height z-score (β = 0.15, 95% CI [0.14, 0.15]). During 2000–2010, the combinations seafood + eggs and seafood + eggs + milk showed the largest effects (β = 0.20, 95% CI [0.19, 0.21]). By 2011–2019, the key combination expanded to “grains + seafood + eggs”, with similar associations observed when milk or fruits were included. Sensitivity analyses using measured average height produced consistent findings (S7 Fig).
Evolution of food consumption patterns
The Kaiser–Meyer–Olkin indices for food consumption data (0.673, 0.824, and 0.717 for 1985–1999, 2000–2010, and 2011–2023) and significant Bartlett’s test (p < 0.001) confirmed the suitability of factor analysis; three principal components were retained in each period (S8 Fig).
Overall, Chinese food consumption evolved from a simple, carbohydrate-based structure to a more balanced and diverse pattern (Fig 3a). From 1985 to 1999, three dominant patterns were identified: high Vegetable oil–eggs (VIE) pattern, high Poultry–seafood–sugar (PEA) pattern, and high Vegetables and mushrooms (VM) pattern. During 2000–2010, the VIE pattern transitioned to Fruits–nuts–milk–eggs–vegetable oil (FUME) pattern; the PEA pattern became Poultry–pork–seafood (PKS) pattern, and a new Beef and mutton–sugar (BUS) pattern appeared. By 2011–2023, the FUME pattern further evolved into the Fruits–nuts–eggs–milk (FUEL) pattern, while the PKS pattern evolved to Pork–poultry–seafood (PLS) pattern with increased pork consumption, and BUS pattern remained largely unchanged. Sensitivity analyses showed that the PCA–derived food consumption patterns were highly stable across alternative rotation methods, with largely consistent major contributing foods and Tucker’s congruence coefficients of 0.99–1.00 for matched components (S4 and S5 Tables).

Advantages of the FUEL pattern
The FUEL pattern was associated with better height outcomes and greater sustainability. From 2011 to 2023, the population following this pattern had the highest mean height and height z-scores (ANOVA and Tukey HSD, both p < 0.001, Fig 3b). Its predecessor, the FUME pattern, showed similar benefits from 2000 to 2010.
After adjustment for provincial GDP per capita, annual mean sunshine duration, annual mean temperature, and provincial-level educational attainment, the associations between principal component scores and height z-scores remained pattern-specific (Fig 4a). During 1985–1999, the PEA pattern showed the strongest positive association with height z-scores (partial ρ = 0.763, 95% CI [0.727, 0.794]; p < 0.001), followed by the VIE pattern (partial ρ = 0.474, 95% CI [0.405, 0.538]; p < 0.001). During 2000–2010, the FUME pattern showed the strongest positive association (partial ρ = 0.765, 95% CI [0.730, 0.794]; p < 0.001), followed by the PKS pattern (partial ρ = 0.309, 95% CI [0.231, 0.384]; p < 0.001). During 2011–2023, the FUEL pattern remained positively associated with height z-scores after adjustment (partial ρ = 0.518, 95% CI [0.453, 0.580]; p < 0.001), meanwhile the PLS pattern showed a weak positive association (partial ρ = 0.089, 95% CI [0.008, 0.170]; p = 0.031). Sensitivity analyses using measured average height produced similar results (S9 Fig). Lagged sensitivity analyses further supported the temporal robustness of these associations (S10–S15 Figs). Across the 1-, 3-, and 5-year lag periods, the VIE and PEA patterns during 1985–1999, the FUME and PKS patterns during 2000–2010, and the FUEL pattern during 2011–2019 remained positively associated with height outcomes. The VM pattern during 1985–1999 and the BUS pattern during 2000–2010 remained not significantly associated with height outcomes, whereas the PLS pattern during 2011–2019 was no longer significantly associated with height outcomes in the lagged analyses. These findings were consistent for both height Z-score and absolute height.

Additional nutrient profiling revealed marked differences in nutrient supply across dietary transition periods and food consumption patterns (S16 Fig, Kruskal–Wallis test, all p < 0.001). Height gains were not associated with a consistent increase in energy or carbohydrate supply. Rather, the height-favorable patterns in each period, including PEA, FUME, and FUEL, were characterized by more favorable nutritional profiles, including higher calcium-to-phosphorus ratios and calcium density (S17–S19 Figs, Kruskal–Wallis test, all p < 0.001).
Consistent with these nutrient profiles, multivariable analyses showed that higher protein, calcium, and zinc densities were positively associated with both height z-score and absolute height across all three periods; fat density showed similarly positive associations (S7 Table). Notably, carbohydrate density was consistently inversely associated with both height outcomes across all three periods. In contrast, the magnitude of the association between total energy and height progressively decreased over time and was no longer statistically significant in 2011–2019.
The FUEL pattern exhibited relatively favorable environmental and economic profiles (Fig 4b). It showed lower greenhouse gas emissions (1,000–1,800 kg CO2-eq per year), moderate land use, reduced acidification (<9,000 g SO2-eq per year), lower eutrophication, and relatively low freshwater demand. Economically, it was also the most cost-effective option in 2010–2023. Overall, the FUEL pattern was the food consumption pattern most consistently associated with greater height z-scores while showing relatively favorable environmental and economic profiles.
FCH score development and validation and FUEL pattern validation
To assess how food consumption contributes to height, we developed a machine-learning model, treating height as a continuous outcome. Among the tested algorithms, the random forest model performed best and was used for subsequent analyses (S20 Fig). We then applied SHAP to estimate the marginal contributions of each food group.
